text: Our detective just stepped in gum, and it won't let go.
So how many pieces of bubble gum would it take to lift a car?
For a whole car, you'd need a million pieces, minimum.
Honestly, my gut said thousands.
Small cars weigh just over a thousand kilos, so let's say twelve hundred.
The answer surprised me, and then it surprised me again.
First clue: a Tokyo study on how badly gum sticks to dentures.
Their recipe: chew a stick's worth of gum for five minutes.
Squish it between two small plates, then pull them apart.
On a dry plastic plate, one piece held about seventeen newtons.
That's like hanging a one-and-a-half-liter water bottle, and then some.
I can't even open that bottle.
Small catch: their gum was xylitol gum, not bubble gum.
Bubble gum tends to be tougher when stretched.
But nobody I could find has measured how well it sticks.
So I'll borrow their number and cross my fingers.
Now the car. If every piece pulls its weight, that's about seven hundred pieces.
Their metal plate says closer to nine hundred.
Not a million, not even a thousand.
I was rounding up. Nine hundred is basically breakfast, so I'll chew them myself.
And he starts chewing all nine hundred. Please don't try that part at home.
But they ran one more test, and it's bad news for all that chewing.
They put a tiny drop of fake spit between the gum and the plate.
On metal, the gum held under one newton on average, less than a hundred grams.
After nine hundred pieces, he's drooled on every metal plate in the lab.
He presses one down, pulls, and it pops right off.
Why does spit do that? Even the researchers only had a guess.
With fake spit on metal, the math jumps to roughly twelve thousand pieces.
Twelve thousand pieces, and my jaw already quit.
So he stops chewing, grabs a hair dryer, and dries the plates.
Dry plates, nine hundred pieces, and one giant pink rope.
Hmm, I wouldn't make it a rope.
He hangs a weight on it, and one spot starts getting skinny.
The whole weight runs through that skinny spot, with the least gum to carry it.
Make that spot half as thick, and it takes four times the stress.
So my rope is just a noodle with ambitions.
Plan B: the gum goes flat, like a pink sandwich between two dry plates.
One plate hangs from a crane, the other is fixed to the car's roof.
That way, all nine hundred share the load side by side.
Will it actually lift? Nobody's tried it, as far as I know, so picture it.
He runs the crane by remote, from way behind the safety line.
Rule one: nobody goes under a lifted car, not here, not in real life.
He presses the button, and the car lifts!
It's up, it's up, case closed!
But nine hundred is just enough, so every piece is near its limit.
My guess: it holds a moment, then lets go without a single snap.
Gum holds like rubber and flows like honey, both at once.
He copies one student's test: chewed gum between two sheets of paper.
A three-hundred-gram weight tugs one sheet sideways.
About seven minutes later, it's slid more than seven centimeters.
That's a whole finger's length, just from waiting.
In the student's notes, a harder pull made it slide much faster. Like, say, a car.
Then I'll just add more gum!
Way more gum would probably make it sink slowly instead.
But slower isn't stopped: it just quietly parks itself again.
So how many pieces does it take to lift a car?
For a quick lift on dry plates, simple math says seven to nine hundred.
To keep it up there forever, I don't think any number is enough.
Which means 'how many' was never the hard part.
It's how many seconds count as a win.
So, nine hundred pieces and somebody really fast with a camera.
Remember the gum on his shoe? He finally walks off, and it still hasn't snapped.
It never needed to be strong, it just needed to keep stretching.
Case closed, very, very, very slowly.
